steps.headline: Build a case for the Government and weigh it against the Opposition's main impact.

workedSteps.text: The motion is "This House would make city buses free", and the Government's claim is that free buses cut car commuting. Give the mechanism and the impact.
workedSteps.math:
Mechanism: with no fare, driving loses its cost edge
Impact: fewer cars, less pollution

workedSteps.text: Put numbers on the impact. Suppose 40,000 commuters could switch, with probability 0.25.
The Opposition's main impact is service cuts that hurt 8,000 riders, with probability 0.5. Work out its expected size on the same scale.
Compare the two, and add the other axes. The Government's is larger by 6,000, and fares could be brought back if cuts began, so the harm is reversible.
Say it as a weighing sentence, conceding what is true.
workedSteps.math: "Even if some services are cut, more people switch and the cuts can be reversed."

steps.headline: Weigh a larger Opposition impact on the same scale.

workedSteps.text: Suppose the Opposition argues instead that the cuts would hurt 12,000 riders, with probability 0.3.
Its expected size goes on the same scale as the Government's 10,000.
The comparison with the Government's 10,000 comes next, along with the other axis, which is that fares can be reintroduced if the cuts begin.

reveal.text: A weighing sentence earns its place by naming axes that a judge can check, and by conceding what is fair.

lessons.orientation: Analyse a motion, build arguments with a mechanism and an impact, and weigh competing impacts by size, probability, timeframe and reversibility.
lessons.nextAction: You can now hear and test an argument, answer questions aloud under a time limit, persuade honestly, and build and weigh a case in a British Parliamentary round.

blocks.text: Suppose one team in a debate claims an impact that would help 1,000 people but has only about a thirty percent chance of happening, while the other team's impact would help 200 people and is almost certain. Each team is right about its own impact, and the judges still have to decide which one matters more.
Rounds like this are usually won by the team that makes the comparison out loud instead of leaving it to the judges.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to analyse a motion, build an argument with a mechanism and an impact, work out the expected size of an impact, and weigh two impacts on size, probability, timeframe and reversibility.
intro.whyItMatters: A case that explains and weighs its impacts gives the judges something to check, and a bare list of claims does not.

recap.keyIdea: Analyse the motion, build each argument with a mechanism and an impact, and weigh your impacts against the other side's on named axes.

blocks.text: A claim with no mechanism is an assertion, and an impact becomes comparable when you put a number on its expected size, the number affected multiplied by the probability. Size is only one axis, so a good weighing also names timeframe and reversibility and concedes what is true on the other side.
A closing team adds an extension, and a recorded 4-minute case scored on role, matter, manner and time shows what to change next.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Hours are cut, prices are up and the town is empty. The mall must go." Which statement is the claim?
hints: Ask which sentence the others are there to support.
Which one tells the listener what to think or do?

choices.label: Prices are up.
The mall must go.
Hours are cut.
The town is empty.

questions.onCorrect: The first sentence is a list of grounds, and the last is what they are offered for. A claim can come last.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the grounds. Ask which statement the three observations are meant to support.
That is a ground, one of three. The claim is what they add up to.
That is a ground too. The claim is the statement the others are offered for.

questions.prompt: In "The shop is dark and the door is locked, so it must be closed", which single word marks the conclusion?
hints: The conclusion is the claim the earlier statements lead to.
Look for the small word between the grounds and the claim.
questions.onCorrect: The word so points forward to the conclusion. Words like therefore and thus do the same job.

misconceptions.feedback: The word and joins the two grounds, the dark shop and the locked door. It does not point ahead to the conclusion.
The word locked belongs to a ground, a fact offered in support. The word that marks the conclusion is a small one that sits between the grounds and the claim.
The word must is part of the conclusion and shows how strongly it is claimed. The word that marks where the conclusion begins comes just before it.

choices.label: and
locked
so
must

questions.prompt: The survey asked 20 staff and 14 preferred 10 a.m. What percentage of the staff surveyed is that?
hints: Divide the number who preferred 10 a.m. by the number asked.
14 ÷ 20 gives a decimal.
Multiply the decimal by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: That is a clear majority of the 20 asked, though the speech does not say how those 20 were chosen.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count, not the share. Divide by the 20 who were asked and write it as a percentage.
That is how many did not prefer 10 a.m. Use the 14 who did.

questions.prompt: "The bridge will probably flood this spring, because the river rose past the same mark twice in the last three years." Is this an explanation or an argument?
hints: Does the listener already accept that the bridge will flood?
Ask whether the speaker is giving a cause or trying to win agreement.
questions.onCorrect: The flood has not happened, so the speaker is offering grounds for believing it will. The word because does not decide the question.

misconceptions.feedback: An explanation gives the cause of something already accepted. A flood that has not happened is still in doubt, so the speaker is arguing for it.

choices.label: An explanation
An argument

questions.prompt: "Most of its users work on weekdays." Is that a claim, a reason or evidence in the library speech?
hints: It supports the claim, but is anything under it?
Is it the thing the speaker wants accepted, or a ground for it?
questions.onCorrect: It is offered as a ground for opening on Sundays, and no fact is given under it, so it stands as a reason without evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: The claim is what the speaker wants accepted, here opening on Sundays. This statement is offered in its support.
Evidence would be a fact or figure under the statement. Here the statement itself is the ground, with nothing under it.

choices.label: A claim
A reason
Evidence

questions.prompt: According to the pool's own records in the speech, how many children take lessons there each week?
hints: Find the figure the speaker attributes to the pool's records.
It is the number under the reason about children.
Read the speech again for the only count it contains.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The speech gives the pool's records as the evidence for the second reason: 400 children each week.

questions.onCorrect: That figure is the evidence under the second reason. The first reason, the 20-mile gap, has none.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a distance, the content of the first reason. The count of children is the evidence for the second.

questions.prompt: Which part of the speech is the evidence under the reason that children rely on the pool?
hints: Evidence is a fact, figure or example that stands under a reason.
Ask which sentence the speaker could show you a source for.

acceptedIdeas: The pool's records of 400 children taking lessons each week.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pool's records of 400 children taking lessons each week.

choices.label: The pool's records of 400 children taking lessons each week.
The town should keep its swimming pool.
It is the only pool within 20 miles.

questions.onCorrect: The records are a fact the speaker can point to, which is what lets them stand under the reason. Reason 1 has nothing under it, and a standard line for this speech would mark that gap.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the recommendation the whole speech supports, so it is the claim.
That is the other reason, a ground offered for the claim, and the speech gives no fact under it.

questions.prompt: A speaker never states a claim but says: "The queue at lunch is twelve minutes long. The café next door serves in four. Half of our regulars haven't been back since March." How many separate grounds does the speaker give?
hints: Read each sentence and ask whether it supports something.
Count the sentences that each offer a separate ground.
The speaker states three facts and no recommendation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the three sentences is its own ground for an unstated claim such as that lunch service is too slow.

questions.onCorrect: All three work together toward a claim the speaker leaves for you to supply, which is that service must get faster.

misconceptions.feedback: The first sentence is only one of three. The others each give a separate ground.
Two of the three is a count of the sentences about the queue and the rival. The third sentence is a ground too.

questions.prompt: A speaker never states a claim but says: "The queue at lunch is twelve minutes long. The café next door serves in four. Half of our regulars haven't been back since March." Which claim are the three sentences pointing to?
hints: Each sentence is a ground. Ask what all three are offered to support.
Think about what the speaker would want done, given these three facts.

acceptedIdeas: Lunch service has to get faster.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Lunch service has to get faster.

choices.label: The café next door has better food.
Lunch service has to get faster.
The regulars have stopped eating lunch.
The queue was shorter before March.

questions.onCorrect: When a claim is left unsaid, supplying it yourself, and checking it with the speaker, is part of hearing the argument.

misconceptions.feedback: None of the sentences mentions food. They are about waiting times and customers who stopped coming, and those point to the speed of service.
The third sentence says the regulars haven't come back here, which is offered as a ground, and it supports a claim about the service that drove them away.
The speaker says nothing about the queue before March. The three facts support a recommendation about how fast lunch is served.

questions.prompt: A councillor says: "Our clinic's waiting list has doubled in a year. We need a second clinic. Nobody can be seen in under three weeks." What is the claim?
hints: Ask which statement the other two are offered to support.
The claim does not have to come first.

choices.label: Nobody can be seen in under three weeks.
We need a second clinic.
The waiting list has doubled in a year.

questions.onCorrect: The two observations are reasons, and the recommendation they support sits in the middle of the speech.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a ground, a fact offered as support. The claim is the statement it supports.
That is a second ground. The claim is what both observations are offered for.

questions.prompt: Everyone in the village can see the café is shut, and the owner says: "It's shut because I'm ill." Is that an argument or an explanation?
hints: Does anyone doubt that the café is shut?
Is the speaker trying to win agreement, or give a cause?
questions.onCorrect: The shutting is already accepted, so the owner is giving its cause rather than supporting a doubtful claim.

misconceptions.feedback: An argument supports a claim in doubt. Everyone can already see the café is shut, so the owner is explaining why.

choices.label: An explanation
An argument

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Trains are unreliable. Nine of the last 30 were more than five minutes late." In this lesson's terms, what is "nine of the last 30"?
hints: It is a fact offered under a reason.
It is neither the claim nor the reason itself.
questions.onCorrect: The count is a fact that stands under the reason that trains are unreliable, which makes it evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: The reason is the statement that trains are unreliable. The count of late trains stands under it.
A claim is what the speaker wants accepted. The count is a fact offered in support of a reason.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Every pupil at Hill School passes their exams, so Hill School must teach well." Which unstated statement does the step from grounds to claim depend on?
hints: The missing statement is a general rule, not a fact about Hill School.
Ask what would have to be true for the grounds to support the claim.

acceptedIdeas: If a school's pupils all pass, its teaching is the reason.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If a school's pupils all pass, its teaching is the reason.

choices.label: Every pupil at Hill School passes their exams.
A school that teaches well has pupils who pass their exams.
If a school's pupils all pass, its teaching is the reason.
Hill School has smaller classes than most schools.

questions.onCorrect: The unsaid rule is the warrant. Without it the grounds say only that the pupils pass, not that the school's teaching is the reason.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs the rule the wrong way round. It starts from good teaching and ends at good results, while the argument starts from the results.
That is the grounds, which the speaker has already said. The missing statement is the rule that carries you from them to the claim.
Small classes might help a school teach well, but the speaker never mentions them. The missing statement links the exam results to the teaching.

questions.prompt: "The restaurant is full every night, so it must serve good food." The unspoken rule that popular restaurants serve good food is this argument's what?
hints: Toulmin's name for the general rule that links grounds to claim.
It is neither the grounds nor the claim.
questions.onCorrect: A warrant is the general rule behind the step, and speakers seldom state it. Here it is a rule you can test, since crowds gather for other reasons too.

misconceptions.feedback: The grounds are the stated fact, that the restaurant is full. The unspoken rule that links that fact to the claim has another name.
The claim is that the food is good. The unspoken rule that carries you to it has another name.

questions.prompt: In "Harry was born in Bermuda, so presumably he is a British subject", what is the word "presumably" called in Toulmin's model?
hints: It sets how strongly the speaker claims the conclusion.
Think of what a word like probably does to a claim.
questions.onCorrect: A qualifier says how strong a claim the speaker is making. "Certainly" claims the most, and "presumably" leaves room for an exception.

misconceptions.feedback: The warrant is the general rule behind the step. The single word that sets the strength of the claim has another name.
An exception is a condition under which the warrant fails. The word that signals how strong the claim is has another name.

questions.prompt: Is the question "Is it the only bakery on this street?" aimed at the grounds or at the warrant of "The queue is always long, so the bread must be the best"?
hints: The grounds are that the queue is long, which nobody doubts.
The question offers another reason a queue might form.

acceptedIdeas: The warrant, because a queue can form for other reasons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The warrant, because a queue can form for other reasons

questions.onCorrect: The queue is not in doubt, but the rule that a long queue means the best bread is, since a queue can form for other reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: The grounds are that the queue is long, and the question does not dispute that. It asks whether a long queue really shows the best bread.

choices.label: The grounds, because it asks whether the queue is really long
The warrant, because a queue can form for other reasons

questions.prompt: Accidents on Station Road fell from 50 a year to 35 after the speed limit was cut. By what percentage did they fall?
hints: Work out how many fewer accidents there were.
Divide that fall by the starting figure, 50.
Turn the decimal into a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: A fall of 30% is a fact about the grounds. Whether the limit caused it is a separate matter.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fall in accidents. Divide it by the starting figure, 50, to get a percentage.
That is 35 as a percentage of 50, the share that remained. Ask how much the figure fell.

questions.prompt: A councillor says: "We cut the limit on Station Road to 20 mph, and accidents there fell from 50 a year to 35, so the cut works." Which statement is the warrant?
hints: The warrant is a general rule, and it is usually left unsaid.
Ask what has to be true for the fall to show that the cut works.

acceptedIdeas: A fall that follows a change was caused by the change.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fall that follows a change was caused by the change.

choices.label: Accidents on Station Road fell from 50 a year to 35.
Station Road had more accidents than other roads.
The cut to 20 mph works.
A fall that follows a change was caused by the change.

questions.onCorrect: Said aloud, the rule invites the obvious exception, that accidents might have been falling anyway.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grounds, the fact the councillor states. The warrant is the unspoken rule that carries that fact to the claim.
That is the claim itself. The warrant is the rule that links the fall in accidents to it.
The councillor never says this, and the argument doesn't need it. What it needs is a rule that turns a fall after the cut into proof that the cut caused it.

questions.prompt: A promoter says: "Tickets will certainly sell out on Saturday, because they sold out last year." A listener asks: "Is this year's venue the same size?" What word names a condition that would make the promoter's reasoning fail?
hints: It is a condition under which the warrant fails.
Toulmin also calls it the rebuttal.
questions.onCorrect: A bigger venue is an exception to the rule that last year's sell-out predicts this year's. Whether it applies here is the question the listener has put.

misconceptions.feedback: The warrant is the general rule that last year's sell-out predicts this year's. A bigger venue is a condition under which that rule fails.
The qualifier is the word that sets the strength, here certainly. A bigger venue is a condition under which the rule fails.

questions.prompt: "Harry was born in Bermuda, so presumably he is a British subject." Which statement is the warrant?
hints: The warrant is a general rule rather than a fact about Harry.
Ask which statement would let you move from the grounds to the claim for any man, not just Harry.

acceptedIdeas: A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.

choices.label: Harry was born in Bermuda.
Harry is a British subject.
Presumably.
A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.

questions.onCorrect: The warrant is the general rule that licenses the step, so it speaks of men born in Bermuda and not of Harry alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grounds, the fact about Harry. The warrant is the general rule that carries you from it to the claim.
That is the claim. The warrant is the rule that links the grounds to it.
That is the qualifier, which sets how strongly the claim is made. The warrant is the rule behind the step.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "In most cases, a new bypass eases traffic in the town centre." What do we call the phrase "in most cases"?
hints: It tells you how strong a claim is being made.
questions.onCorrect: The phrase marks how strong the claim is, and by allowing for cases where it fails it makes the speaker harder to refute.

misconceptions.feedback: An exception is a specific condition under which the rule fails. A phrase that sets the strength of a claim has another name.

questions.prompt: A listener asks the gym speaker: "Did you count the members who left?" Which part of the argument is that question aimed at?
hints: The question asks whether the stated fact is complete.
Which part says that everyone at the gym is fit?
questions.onCorrect: Counting only the members who stayed could make the gym look better than it is, so the question tests whether the facts are complete.

misconceptions.feedback: The warrant is the general rule behind the step. This question asks whether the stated facts are complete, so it tests the facts.
An exception is a condition under which the warrant fails, such as a gym that admits only people who are already fit. This question asks whether the facts offered are complete.

choices.label: The grounds
The warrant
An exception

questions.prompt: "You can't trust his tax plan; he has been divorced twice." What is the name of this move?
hints: The reply is about the man, not about the plan.
The Latin phrase means "to the person".
questions.onCorrect: The marriage history says nothing about whether the plan's figures add up, so the reply answers the person and leaves the plan untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: A straw man distorts what was said. Nothing in the plan was misstated here; the reply left the plan alone and turned to the person.
A false dilemma offers only two options. This reply offers no options; it turns to the speaker's private life.

questions.prompt: Someone presents a tax plan, and a listener replies: "You can't trust his tax plan; he has been divorced twice." What does the reply actually answer?
hints: Set the reply beside the proposal and ask what it is about.
Does the reply mention anything in the plan?

acceptedIdeas: The man who proposed the plan.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The man who proposed the plan.

choices.label: Whether the plan is affordable.
An exaggerated version of the plan.
The figures in the tax plan.
The man who proposed the plan.

questions.onCorrect: His divorces would matter only if the question were about him, and the question is about the plan.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply mentions no figures at all. It is about the man's divorces, which say nothing about the plan.
Nothing in the reply touches cost. It talks about the man's private life instead.
The reply doesn't restate the plan in any form, exaggerated or not. It leaves the plan aside and talks about the man.

questions.prompt: A says: "We should keep the library open an hour later." B replies: "So you want to waste public money on an empty building?" What is the name of B's move?
hints: Compare what A said with what B says A said.
A is attacked for something A never proposed.
questions.onCorrect: A asked for one more hour, and B answers a different and weaker position, that the building will stand empty.

misconceptions.feedback: B does not attack A as a person. B attacks a distorted version of A's proposal.
B does not offer two options. B swaps A's proposal for a weaker one.

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "Everyone in the office hates the new rota." The speaker asked 3 of the 60 staff. What percentage of the staff was asked?
hints: Divide the number asked by the number of staff.
3 ÷ 60 is a small decimal.
Multiply the decimal by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Five percent is a thin sample, and the three people asked may not be typical, so "everyone" is a broad conclusion from few cases.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of people asked. Divide it by the 60 on the staff to get a percentage.
That is 60 ÷ 3, the wrong way round. Divide the number asked by the whole staff.

questions.prompt: A councillor proposes keeping the library open an hour later, and someone says: "Of course he wants it; he lives next door." Which reply best returns the discussion to the argument?
hints: A good reply says what was done and then points at the next thing to examine.
Which options keep the later closing time under discussion?

acceptedIdeas: Where I live doesn't show whether people would use the extra hour. Can we check the visitor counts?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Where I live doesn't show whether people would use the extra hour. Can we check the visitor counts?

choices.label: I do live next door, as it happens, and I like the library very much, so I see why it matters to me.
You're wrong, and you know it. You only oppose it because you have never once used the library.
That's a straw man, and it is unfair of you to say it, so I'd ask you to withdraw the remark now.
Where I live doesn't show whether people would use the extra hour. Can we check the visitor counts?

questions.onCorrect: The reply says briefly what the remark was about and hands the room a concrete question about the extra hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That names the wrong move, since nothing the speaker said was distorted, and a label alone gives the room nothing to check.
That is another attack, and it hands the room a quarrel in place of a question about the library.
That answers the personal point and leaves the library alone. The reply should send the discussion back to the proposal.

questions.prompt: "Either we ban all cars from the town centre or we accept filthy air." What is the name of this move?
hints: Count the options the speaker allows.
Are there choices between a total ban and doing nothing?
questions.onCorrect: The speaker allows two options only, and a charge or a low-emission zone sits between them.

misconceptions.feedback: A straw man distorts someone's position. Here nobody's view has been restated; two options have been offered as if they were the only ones.

questions.prompt: A proposes a 20 mph limit near the school. B replies: "So you want everyone to crawl everywhere at 20?" Which word has B added that A never said?
hints: Compare A's "near the school" with B's version.
B widens the place where the limit applies.
questions.onCorrect: A asked for a limit near the school. B stretches it to every road, which is easy to knock down and is not what A proposed.

misconceptions.feedback: Everyone widens the people affected, but the clearest change is in place. Compare A's near the school with the place B names.

questions.prompt: A says: "The bypass will cut journey times; everybody says so." B replies: "That's a bandwagon argument, so the bypass won't cut journey times." What name is given to B's error?
hints: B has shown that one reason is weak.
Has B shown that the claim itself is false?
questions.onCorrect: Saying that everybody agrees is a weak reason, but the bypass may still cut journey times for other reasons, which B has not examined.

misconceptions.feedback: B does not distort A's claim. B treats a weak reason as proof that the claim is false.
B does not attack A personally. B treats a weak reason as proof that the claim is false.

questions.prompt: "Two of my friends tried the new app and both lost their data, so the app destroys data." What is the name of this move?
hints: Count the cases the conclusion rests on.
How wide is the conclusion compared with two friends?
questions.onCorrect: A conclusion about the whole app rests on two friends, who may have hit a rare fault that most users never meet.

misconceptions.feedback: A straw man distorts what someone said. Nobody's position is distorted here, because a wide conclusion is drawn from two cases.
A false dilemma limits the options to two. This speaker draws a wide conclusion from two cases.

questions.prompt: "Either we sign the contract today or we lose the client." What is the name of this move?
hints: The speaker allows exactly two outcomes.
Is there anything between signing today and losing the client?
questions.onCorrect: Asking for a week, or signing with changes, falls between the two options the speaker allowed.

misconceptions.feedback: Nobody is attacked personally here. Only two options are allowed, when others exist.
No one's position is distorted here. Two options are offered as if they were the only ones.

questions.prompt: Someone gives a bad argument for a claim. What can you conclude about the claim?
hints: A fallacy removes one support for the claim.
Ask whether other support might exist.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing yet, because other grounds may exist.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing yet, because other grounds may exist.

choices.label: It is probably false, because its support failed.
It is false, because the argument for it failed.
Nothing yet, because other grounds may exist.
It is true, because nobody has refuted it.

questions.onCorrect: A bad argument removes that support and nothing more, so the claim stands or falls on whatever else can be said for it.

misconceptions.feedback: A fallacy shows that one argument fails. The claim may still be true for other reasons.
A bad argument gives no reason to think the claim true, and a claim is not true just because it has not been refuted. It leaves the question open.
A bad argument for a claim says nothing about how probable the claim is. It leaves the question open.

questions.prompt: Taking a pill raises the risk of a clot from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000, which a headline reports as a 50 percent rise. Roughly how many extra women in each 1,000 does the rise affect?
hints: Compare the two risks per 1,000 directly.
The 50 percent is measured against the starting 2, and not against 1,000.

choices.label: About 50
About 150
Just 1
About 500

questions.onCorrect: One extra case per 1,000 is the absolute change, and the 50 percent in the headline is the same change as a share of the starting 2.

misconceptions.feedback: The 50 percent is a share of the starting risk of 2 in 1,000, and not a share of all women, so the rise is from 2 cases to 3.
Fifty extra would mean the risk went from 2 to 52 in 1,000, while here it goes from 2 to 3.
Going from 2 to 3 in 1,000 adds one case in each 1,000, far fewer than 150.

questions.prompt: A treatment cuts risk from 10 in 1,000 to 7 in 1,000. By what percent has the risk fallen, relative to the starting figure?
hints: Find the fall in the number of cases first.
Divide the fall by the starting number of cases, 10.
Write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fall is 3, and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3, which is 30% of the starting figure.

questions.onCorrect: A fall of 30 percent sounds large, even though only 3 people in 1,000 are affected by the change.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the absolute fall, 3 cases in 1,000. Divide it by the starting 10 to get the relative fall.
That is the fall in percentage points. The question asks for the relative fall as a percent of the start.

questions.prompt: Unemployment rises from 5 percent to 8 percent. By what percent, relative to the starting figure, has it risen?
hints: Find the rise in percentage points first.
Divide the rise by the starting percentage, 5.
Write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 3 points, and 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6, which is 60%.

questions.onCorrect: The rise is 3 percentage points and 60 percent in relative terms, and a speaker who gives only one of those figures has told you half the story.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in percentage points. The question asks for the rise relative to the start, which means dividing by 5.
That divides by the end figure, 8. Relative change is measured against the starting figure.

questions.prompt: "Six people were hurt on the new slide." Suppose 12,000 people used it. How many were hurt per 1,000 users?
hints: Divide the number hurt by the number of users.
Scale the result to 1,000 users by multiplying by 1,000.
6 ÷ 12 gives the same answer, because 12,000 is 12 thousands.
questions.onCorrect: Half a person per 1,000 users is a rate you can compare with other slides, which is what the number six alone could never be.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of people hurt. Divide by the number of users, in thousands.
That is 12,000 ÷ 6, the wrong way round. Divide the number hurt by the number of users.

questions.prompt: The risk rises by 0.1 percentage points, which is 1 extra case per 1,000. How many extra cases is that among 100,000 women taking the pill?
hints: How many thousands are there in 100,000?
Multiply the extra cases per 1,000 by that number.
1 × 100 gives the answer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 per 1,000 is 100 per 100,000, because 100,000 is 100 thousands.

questions.onCorrect: Putting the change on a larger population gives listeners a figure they can picture: 100 people, in a town of 100,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure per 1,000. There are 100 thousands in 100,000.
That treats 100,000 as 10 thousands. Count how many thousands there are.

questions.prompt: Unemployment rose from 5 percent to 6 percent. By what percent, relative to the starting figure, did it rise?
hints: Find the rise in percentage points.
Divide it by the starting percentage, 5.
Write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 1 point, and 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2, which is 20%.

questions.onCorrect: Said with both figures: unemployment rose by one percentage point, from 5 to 6 percent, which is a 20 percent rise on where it started. The same point would be a 25 percent rise from 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in percentage points. Divide it by the starting 5 to get the relative rise.
That divides by the end figure, 6. Relative change is measured against the starting figure.

questions.prompt: A forum poll gets 50 votes from the 400 staff, and 40 of the voters say they read the newsletter, so the speaker claims that 80 percent of staff read it. What percentage of all 400 staff voted at all?
hints: The number who voted is 50, out of 400 staff.
Divide 50 by 400.
Write the decimal as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Only one staff member in eight voted, and those who choose to vote in a newsletter poll are likely to be the ones who read it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of voters who said yes. The question asks what share of all staff voted.
That is 400 ÷ 50, the wrong way round. Divide the voters by all 400 staff.

questions.prompt: A screening programme lowers a risk from 5 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. By how many percentage points does the risk fall?
hints: Write each risk as a percentage first.
5 in 1,000 is 0.5 percent, and 3 in 1,000 is 0.3 percent.
Subtract the two percentages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 in 1,000 is 0.5% and 3 in 1,000 is 0.3%, so the fall is 0.2 percentage points.

questions.onCorrect: The risk falls by 0.2 percentage points, which is 2 in 1,000 and a relative fall of 40 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the relative fall, a share of the starting risk. The question asks for the fall in percentage points.
That is the fall per 1,000. Write each risk as a percentage, then subtract, to get percentage points.

questions.prompt: A pass rate rises from 60 percent to 66 percent. By what percent has it risen, relative to the starting figure?
hints: Find the rise in percentage points.
Divide the rise by the starting percentage, 60.
Write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 6 points, and 6 ÷ 60 = 0.1, which is 10%.

questions.onCorrect: The pass rate rose by 6 percentage points, which is a relative rise of 10 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in percentage points. Divide by the starting 60 to get the relative rise.
That divides by the end figure, 66. Relative change is measured against the starting figure.

questions.prompt: "Six people were hurt on the new slide." What do you most need to know to judge this?
hints: A count means little without what it is a count of.
Which missing number would let you work out a rate?

acceptedIdeas: How many people used the slide.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How many people used the slide.

choices.label: The date it opened.
How tall the slide is.
How many people used the slide.
Who built it.

questions.onCorrect: The number who used the slide is the denominator, and it turns a count into a rate you can compare.

misconceptions.feedback: The height might matter for safety, but six injuries mean little until you know what they are six out of.
The builder may matter later, but the count alone still has nothing to compare it with.
The opening date matters only alongside something else. First the six injuries need something to be measured against.

questions.prompt: A speaker proposes a four-day week on full pay. A critic replies: "So you want everyone to stop working on Fridays and let the company fall behind?" What do we call attacking a weaker, distorted version of the other side's view?
hints: The critic answers a version of the proposal that nobody made.
A man made of straw is easy to knock down.
questions.onCorrect: The proposal was the same work in four days. The critic knocked down a different position, which is why the reply convinces nobody who heard the original.

misconceptions.feedback: A steelman is the opposite: the strongest fair version of the view. The critic's reply is a weaker, distorted version.
The critic does not attack the speaker personally. The reply distorts the proposal.

questions.prompt: A speaker proposes that staff work from home two days a week. Which restatement of the proposal would its supporters accept as fair?
hints: Ask which version the supporters would sign off.
A fair restatement gives the view's best reasons.

acceptedIdeas: They think the same work can be done at home, and that quiet days and lower costs help the firm.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They think the same work can be done at home, and that quiet days and lower costs help the firm.

choices.label: They want the office to stand empty two days a week, whatever that does to the firm and its clients.
They think the same work can be done at home, and that quiet days and lower costs help the firm.
They think the office is a waste, because nobody who works there gets any proper work done.
They want to stay at home and do less, because they find the office tiring and the work dull.

questions.onCorrect: A steelman gives the proposal's strongest reasons in terms its supporters would use, so it is the version worth answering.

misconceptions.feedback: That reduces the proposal to a wish for less work. Its supporters would reject it, because it leaves out their reasons.
That is a caricature. Its supporters would not recognise their case in it.
That distorts the proposal, which is about the same work done at home on two days. It is a straw man.

questions.prompt: In Rapoport's rules as Dennett retells them, how many steps come before you are allowed to rebut?
hints: Count the steps in the ladder before the one marked rebut.
There are four steps in total.
The last step is the rebuttal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Restating, listing agreement and saying what you learned are three steps, and the rebuttal is fourth.

questions.onCorrect: Three steps come first, and in a timed speech you can often fit them into a sentence or two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total number of steps. The rebuttal is the fourth, so three come before it.
The restatement is only the first. Two more steps come before the rebuttal.

questions.prompt: In Rapoport's rules as Dennett retells them, what must you do before you say a word of rebuttal?
hints: The first three rules are all about the other person's view.
Rebuttal is the fourth and last rule.

acceptedIdeas: Restate their position fairly, list where you agree and say what you have learned from them.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Restate their position fairly, list where you agree and say what you have learned from them.

choices.label: State your own position first.
Restate their position fairly, list where you agree and say what you have learned from them.
Name any fallacy the other person has committed.
Concede their whole claim.

questions.onCorrect: Done briefly, all three can fit into a sentence or two before the rebuttal, which is then far easier for the other side to hear.

misconceptions.feedback: Naming fallacies is not one of the rules. They begin with the other person's view, stated fairly.
The rules ask you to list points of agreement, which is much narrower than conceding the claim, and the rebuttal still follows.
Your own view waits until the fourth step, since the first three are all about theirs.

questions.prompt: "The new bus lane will cut commuting time. A trial last August took 12 minutes off a 40-minute trip." A critic points out that schools were shut and roads were quiet in August. Which rebuttal move is the critic making?
hints: The critic questions the trial itself.
The trial is the fact the claim rests on.
questions.onCorrect: The critic says the trial's conditions were not typical, which questions the evidence itself and leaves the logic of the claim alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The link is the rule connecting the trial to the claim. The critic does not dispute that rule, only that the trial's conditions were typical.
An exception names a case where the claim cannot hold, such as a front desk that must open five days. This critic questions whether the trial itself was typical.
Conceding grants the other side's point and weighs it against yours. This critic grants nothing and questions the trial.

choices.label: Deny the evidence
Deny the link
Give an exception
Concede and outweigh

questions.prompt: A speaker says: "The new tram will double ridership. Prove me wrong." Who carries the burden of proof?
hints: The burden lies on whoever makes the claim.
Who has said something surprising?
questions.onCorrect: The burden rests on whoever makes the claim, and it grows with how surprising the claim is. "Prove me wrong" tries to hand it to the listener.

misconceptions.feedback: "Prove me wrong" tries to move the burden, but it stays with the person who made the claim.

choices.label: The speaker
The listener

questions.prompt: The trial took 12 minutes off a 40-minute journey. What percentage of the journey did it save?
hints: Divide the minutes saved by the original journey time.
12 ÷ 40 is a decimal.
Write the decimal as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: A saving of 30 percent is large, which is why the sample matters: one week in August may not carry over to the rest of the year.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the minutes saved. Divide by the 40-minute journey to get a percentage.
That is the new journey time in minutes. Divide the saving by the original time.

questions.prompt: Granting a point you cannot dispute, and then arguing that your side outweighs it, is called making what?
hints: The word comes from conceding something.
It gains credibility, because you have admitted what you cannot defend.
questions.onCorrect: A concession lets you argue from strength, since you have admitted the cost and still explained why your side should win.

misconceptions.feedback: A rebuttal is any answer to the other side. Granting a point and then weighing your side against it has a narrower name.

questions.prompt: A speaker says every shop should close on Sundays, because it worked for a supermarket chain's 40 branches. You run a hospital pharmacy. Which rebuttal move fits best?
hints: Your case is one where the rule would not hold.
Which move names a condition under which the rule fails?

acceptedIdeas: Give an exception: a hospital pharmacy has to stay open.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give an exception: a hospital pharmacy has to stay open.

choices.label: Deny the evidence: the figures from the 40 branches are wrong.
Give an exception: a hospital pharmacy has to stay open.
Concede the claim entirely: the branches did well.
Attack the motives: the speaker may want the shops closed.

questions.onCorrect: A pharmacy that serves patients on Sundays is a case where the warrant fails, which is what an exception names.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing suggests the branch figures are wrong. Your point is that the rule does not cover your case.
Conceding the whole claim abandons the one point you have. The pharmacy is a case where the rule fails.
Attacking the speaker's motives is an ad hominem. The pharmacy gives you a better point about the rule.

questions.prompt: What do we call the strongest fair version of the other side's case, stated so that its supporters would accept it?
hints: It is the opposite of a straw man.
It is made of steel instead of straw.
questions.onCorrect: A steelman makes your reply harder to dismiss, because it answers the best version of the view.

misconceptions.feedback: A straw man is the distorted version. The term for the strongest fair version is its opposite.

questions.prompt: A speaker's evidence comes from a single week in August. Which rebuttal move fits best?
hints: The weak point is how typical the evidence is.
Which move questions the facts the claim rests on?

acceptedIdeas: Deny the evidence: it may not be typical
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deny the evidence: it may not be typical

choices.label: Give an exception: the claim fails in some cases
Deny the link: the evidence does not support the claim
Concede and outweigh: grant the point and weigh it
Deny the evidence: it may not be typical

questions.onCorrect: A single week in August may not be typical, so the fair rebuttal questions whether the evidence represents the rest of the year.

misconceptions.feedback: The link is the rule from the evidence to the claim. A single August week does not attack that rule; it questions whether the evidence is typical.
An exception names a case where the claim cannot hold at all. Here the question is whether one week is typical of the year.
Conceding grants the point, and the weakness here is in the evidence itself, so there is nothing yet to grant.

questions.prompt: What do we call the duty to give reasons for a claim, which rests on whoever makes it?
hints: It rises with how strong and surprising the claim is.
questions.onCorrect: The more surprising the claim, the more support it needs, and saying "prove me wrong" does not move that duty to the listener.

misconceptions.feedback: A steelman is a fair restatement. The duty to give reasons for a claim is called something else.

questions.prompt: A listener asks: "Should we move to a four-day week?" You think yes. Where in your reply should the yes go?
hints: Listeners cannot skim ahead to find the answer.
What would you want to hear if you could not read on?

choices.label: At the end, after the reasons have built up to it.
First, before the reasons.
In the middle, between two reasons.

questions.onCorrect: A listener who hears the point first knows what the reasons are for, and can follow them with that in mind.

misconceptions.feedback: Building up to the answer suits the speaker, who knows where it is going, while a listener who can't skim ahead hears every reason without knowing what it is for.
By the middle the listener has already heard a reason without knowing what it supports, so the answer does most good at the start.

questions.prompt: In PREP, the answer comes first and is stated again at the end. What does the letter P stand for?
hints: The first and last parts of the pattern are the same kind of statement.
It is the answer to the question.
questions.onCorrect: The pattern is Point, Reason, Example, Point: the answer, why, a case, and the answer again.

misconceptions.feedback: The reason and the example supply the support. The P is the answer itself, stated at the start and again at the end.

questions.prompt: Words such as "first", "second" and "so" that tell listeners where they are in your answer are called what?
hints: You met them in the first lesson, from the listener's side.
They mark where you are, like signs on a road.
questions.onCorrect: Placing signposts yourself is what lets a listener who cannot reread keep track of where the answer has reached.

misconceptions.feedback: The points are what you are saying. The words that tell listeners where they are in it have another name.

questions.prompt: A 2-minute answer uses a 15-second opening, a 15-second close and three equal points. How many seconds does each point get?
hints: Convert 2 minutes to seconds.
Take away the opening and the close.
Divide what is left by three.
questions.onCorrect: Each point gets 30 seconds, which is long enough for a claim and a reason but not for a long digression.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for all three points together. Divide it by three.
That divides the full 120 seconds by three. The opening and close take their share first.

questions.prompt: At about 150 words a minute, roughly how many words is a 90-second answer?
hints: Convert 90 seconds to minutes.
Multiply the minutes by 150.
1.5 × 150 is 150 plus half of 150.
questions.onCorrect: About 225 words is shorter than most people expect, which is why a spoken answer has to be planned, not written out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of words in one minute. A 90-second answer is a minute and a half.
That multiplies 90 by 1.5 without converting. Convert 90 seconds to minutes, then multiply by 150.

questions.prompt: At 150 words a minute, how many words fit in a 30-second slot?
hints: 30 seconds is what fraction of a minute?
Take that fraction of 150.
Half of 150.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 seconds is half a minute, so 150 ÷ 2 = 75 words.

questions.onCorrect: A 30-second point is about 75 words, which is roughly a claim, a reason and a sentence of detail.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a whole minute's worth. A 30-second slot is half a minute.
That treats the seconds as words. At 150 words a minute, a half minute holds half of 150.

questions.prompt: A 3-minute answer has a 15-second opening, a 15-second close and three equal points, which get 50 seconds each. At 150 words a minute, how many words does each point get?
hints: How many words per second is 150 words a minute?
150 ÷ 60 is 2.5 words a second.
Multiply 2.5 by 50 seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 seconds is 50 ÷ 60 of a minute, so 150 × 50 ÷ 60 = 125 words. Equivalently, 150 words a minute is 2.5 words a second, and 50 × 2.5 = 125.

questions.onCorrect: Each point gets about 125 words, which is a small paragraph spoken aloud.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the seconds, not the words. Convert at 2.5 words a second.
That is the words in 30 seconds. Each point gets 50 seconds.

questions.prompt: Your slot is cut to 90 seconds. You keep a 15-second opening and a 15-second close, with three equal points. How many seconds does each point get now?
hints: Take away the opening and the close.
Divide what is left by three.
questions.onCorrect: At 20 seconds a point is only about 50 words, which is why a shorter slot means choosing the strongest three points and not squeezing in a fourth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for a 2-minute slot. This slot is 90 seconds, so less time remains for the points.
That is the time for all three points together. Divide it by three.

questions.prompt: In the PREP pattern, what does the P at the end of the answer stand for?
hints: PREP is Point, Reason, Example, Point.
The last part repeats the answer from the first part.

choices.label: Persuasion
Proof
Point, restated
Practice

questions.onCorrect: The last P closes the loop by restating the point the answer began with, which is the sentence a listener is most likely to remember.

misconceptions.feedback: Practice is not a part of the pattern. The last P restates the answer.
Persuasion is a goal of speaking, not a part of the pattern. The last P restates the answer.
Proof would be the reason and example already given. The last P restates the answer.

questions.prompt: A 4-minute answer has a 30-second opening, a 30-second close and three equal points. How many seconds does each point get?
hints: Convert 4 minutes to seconds.
Take away the opening and the close.
Divide what is left by three.
questions.onCorrect: Each point gets a full minute, which is about 150 words.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for the three points together. Divide it by three.
That divides the full 240 seconds by three. The opening and the close take their share first.

questions.prompt: At about 150 words a minute, roughly how many words is a 2-minute-30-second answer?
hints: Convert 2 minutes 30 seconds to minutes.
30 seconds is half a minute, so the time is 2.5 minutes.
Multiply by 150.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 minutes 30 seconds is 2.5 minutes, and 2.5 × 150 = 375 words.

questions.onCorrect: A 2-minute-30-second answer is about 375 words, roughly one page of speech.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 minutes only. The extra 30 seconds adds half a minute.
That is for 3 minutes. 2 minutes 30 seconds is 2.5 minutes.

questions.prompt: A recording of a talk has 450 words and lasts 3 minutes. Roughly how fast was the speaker talking?
hints: Share the 450 words out across the 3 minutes.
Each minute holds about a third of the words.

choices.label: About 150 words a minute
About 450 words a minute
About 50 words a minute
About 1,350 words a minute

questions.onCorrect: Words divided by minutes gives the rate, and 150 a minute sits near the middle of ordinary conversational speech.

misconceptions.feedback: At 50 words a minute, 3 minutes would hold only 150 words, and this recording holds three times that.
That is 450 multiplied by 3. The 450 words are spread over 3 minutes, so each minute holds fewer of them.
450 is the total for all 3 minutes, and each minute holds about a third of it.

questions.prompt: A talk of 3 minutes contains 18 fillers such as "um" and "like". How many fillers per minute is that?
hints: Filler rate is fillers divided by minutes.
Divide 18 by 3.
questions.onCorrect: Six a minute is one every ten seconds, which is a rate a listener starts to notice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total count. Divide it by the 3 minutes.
That multiplies. A rate per minute divides the count by the minutes.

questions.prompt: You set a target of 2 fillers a minute for a 4-minute talk. How many fillers in total does the target allow?
hints: The target is a rate, so the total is the rate times the time.
Multiply 2 by 4.
questions.onCorrect: A target given as a rate converts to a total by multiplying by the length, which tells you what to count in a recording.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate. The total is the rate times the 4 minutes.
That divides the rate by the minutes. Multiply instead.

questions.prompt: Before a talk, a speaker feels nervous. Going by Alison Wood Brooks's 2014 studies, what is it better to tell yourself?
hints: Nerves and the other feeling both involve a racing heart.
The advice was to relabel the feeling rather than lower it.
questions.onCorrect: Anxiety and excitement both involve high arousal, so relabelling the state is a smaller step than trying to bring it down.

misconceptions.feedback: Calm was the comparison group's instruction, and those people did worse. Anxiety and excitement are both high-energy states, so relabelling the feeling is a smaller step than lowering it.
That denies the feeling, which is another way of trying to lower it. The advantage in the studies went to people who relabelled the feeling instead.
That is reassurance, which also aims to lower the feeling. The advantage in the studies went to people who relabelled the feeling instead.

choices.label: I should try to calm down
I am excited
I am not nervous
It will be over in a few minutes

questions.prompt: A 2-minute recording has 310 words and 9 fillers. How many fillers a minute is that?
hints: Filler rate is fillers divided by minutes.
Divide 9 by 2.
questions.onCorrect: At 4.5 a minute the filler rate is high enough to be the one thing to work on first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Divide it by the 2 minutes.
That is the pace in words a minute. The question asks about fillers.

questions.prompt: A 4-minute recording has 560 words and 12 fillers. What is the pace in words per minute?
hints: Pace is words divided by minutes.
Divide 560 by 4.
questions.onCorrect: A pace of 140 is inside a comfortable band, and the 12 fillers, 3 a minute, are the thing to work on.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the word count. Divide it by the 4 minutes.
That is the filler rate, 12 ÷ 4. The question asks for the pace in words.

questions.prompt: A 7-minute speech at 140 words a minute is about how many words?
hints: Words equal pace times minutes.
Multiply 7 by 140.
questions.onCorrect: Running the same relation backwards turns a pace and a time into a word budget, as in the last lesson.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 140 by 7. Multiply the pace by the minutes.
That adds 7 and 140. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A recording has 520 words and lasts 4 minutes. What is the pace in words per minute?
hints: Pace is words divided by minutes.
Divide 520 by 4.
questions.onCorrect: At 130 words a minute the speaker is well within the range of conversational speech.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the word count. Divide it by the 4 minutes.
That multiplies. A rate divides the words by the minutes.

questions.prompt: A talk of 2 minutes 30 seconds contains 15 fillers. How many fillers a minute is that?
hints: Convert 2 minutes 30 seconds to minutes.
The time is 2.5 minutes.
Divide 15 by 2.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 minutes 30 seconds is 2.5 minutes, and 15 ÷ 2.5 = 6 fillers a minute.

questions.onCorrect: Six a minute is one every ten seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 15 by 2. The time is 2.5 minutes, since 30 seconds is half a minute.
That divides 15 by 3. The time is 2.5 minutes.

questions.prompt: What word names the clear formation of consonants, as distinct from the volume carried by breath?
hints: Volume is projection. This is the other half.
It is about the consonants.
questions.onCorrect: Projection carries the sound to the back of the room, and articulation makes the words recognisable once they get there.

misconceptions.feedback: Projection is the volume carried by breath. The clear formation of consonants has another name.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks: "Isn't this just a way to cut jobs?" Which answer deals best with the question?
hints: A good answer deals with the worry first, then moves on.
Check whether each option says "cut jobs" in your own voice.

acceptedIdeas: No one will lose their job under this plan. What matters is that the weekend service stays open.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No one will lose their job under this plan. What matters is that the weekend service stays open.

choices.label: I'd rather talk about the weekend service, which is what really matters here, so let me tell you about that.
Our plan isn't just a way to cut jobs. It's a way of keeping the weekend service open for every family in the county.
I'm not going to comment on jobs today, and I'd ask you to move on to the next question.
No one will lose their job under this plan. What matters is that the weekend service stays open.

questions.onCorrect: The answer takes the worry seriously and gives a real answer to it before it moves to the message, and it never repeats the loaded phrase.

misconceptions.feedback: That moves to the message without answering, so a listener hears evasion.
That repeats "cut jobs" in your own voice, which carries the loaded premise into your answer.
Listeners tend to hear a refusal to comment as concealment, which is worse than a plain answer.

questions.prompt: A key message is "The library stays open at weekends and nobody loses a job." How many words is it?
hints: Count each word, including the small ones.
There are six words up to weekends.
Five more follow: and, nobody, loses, a, job.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The, library, stays, open, at, weekends, and, nobody, loses, a, job: 11 words.

questions.onCorrect: Eleven words is under the limit of 20, so it can be said in one breath and remembered.

misconceptions.feedback: That misses one word. Count every word, including a and at.
That counts one word too many. Check that each word is counted once.

questions.prompt: A hospital is moving its appointments to online booking. Which of these would work as its key message, within this course's working limit of 20 words or fewer?
hints: A key message is short enough to say in one breath.
It should say something definite that a listener could repeat.

acceptedIdeas: "Every patient can now book online, and no clinic is closing."
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: "Every patient can now book online, and no clinic is closing."

choices.label: "No comment on clinic closures."
"The system, which was agreed after months of consultation with doctors, nurses, unions and patients across the county, lets every patient book online."
"We care deeply about patients and the communities they serve."
"Every patient can now book online, and no clinic is closing."

questions.onCorrect: At eleven words it can be said in one breath, and it gives the listener two facts they can check and repeat.

misconceptions.feedback: It is short enough, but it says nothing about the plan that a listener could check or repeat.
That runs to 23 words and buries the point under the process, so it can't be said in one breath.
That leaves the question of closures open and tends to be heard as concealment, while a key message says what you want the listener to keep.

questions.prompt: In the ABC method, the B is the short phrase that moves from your answer to your message, such as "what matters is". What does B stand for?
hints: The phrase carries you across from one part to the other.
Think of what links two banks of a river.
questions.onCorrect: A bridge is a short phrase, used once, and it works only after a real answer.

misconceptions.feedback: The B is not about blame. It is the short phrase that moves you from your answer to your message.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks: "Did the system fail on Saturday?" It did. What should the first word of your answer be?
hints: It asks about a plain fact, and it has two possible answers.
A direct question deserves a direct answer.
questions.onCorrect: A direct question about a fact needs the plain answer before any bridge, because a listener will not hear the bridge until the question has been answered.

misconceptions.feedback: A direct question about a fact deserves the plain answer first, and a bridge only afterwards.

questions.prompt: The key message "Weekend opening stays and every job is kept" is how many words long?
hints: Count each word.
The first part, Weekend opening stays and, is four words.
Every job is kept adds four more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Weekend, opening, stays, and, every, job, is, kept: 8 words.

questions.onCorrect: Eight words is well under the limit of 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That misses one word. Count every word, including and and is.
That counts one word too many. Count each word once.

questions.prompt: The key message "Saturday service is restored and no data was lost" is how many words long?
hints: Count each word.
Saturday service is restored is four words.
And no data was lost adds five.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Saturday, service, is, restored, and, no, data, was, lost: 9 words.

questions.onCorrect: Nine words is well under the limit of 20, and it can be said in a few seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That misses one word. Count every word.
That counts one word too many. Count each word once.

questions.prompt: The system failed on Saturday, and you have answered "Yes, it did." Which key message should follow the bridge?
hints: The message is the one thing listeners should keep.
Which option tells them where things stand now?

acceptedIdeas: "Saturday service is restored and no data was lost."
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: "Saturday service is restored and no data was lost."

choices.label: "The system did not really fail on Saturday."
"We apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused."
"Saturday service is restored and no data was lost."

questions.onCorrect: At nine words it fits well inside the limit, and it tells listeners the two things they most want to know.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes back the yes you have just given, and a listener will hear the contradiction before anything else.
An apology can belong in the acknowledgement, but it tells the listener nothing about where things stand now, which is the message's job.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks how many jobs will go, and you do not yet know the final figure. Which answer keeps your credibility?
hints: An honest answer says what you do not know and what happens next.
Which options claim knowledge you do not have?

acceptedIdeas: I don't know the final figure yet, and I'll confirm it by Friday.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: I don't know the final figure yet, and I'll confirm it by Friday.

choices.label: I don't know the final figure yet, and I'll confirm it by Friday.
None, I'm certain of it.
No comment.
Fewer than most people think.

questions.onCorrect: Saying that you do not know, and when you will, is honest, and a speaker who does this is believed when they do know.

misconceptions.feedback: Listeners hear no comment as concealment, and it gives them nothing.
That claims knowledge you do not have, and a later figure would damage your credibility.
That sounds like an answer but gives no figure, and listeners notice the evasion.

questions.prompt: In the ABC method, what does the A stand for?
hints: It is the first step, before the bridge.
It deals with the question that was asked.
questions.onCorrect: The first step deals with the question asked, so that the bridge that follows is earned.

misconceptions.feedback: The bridge is the second step. The first deals with the question that was asked.

questions.prompt: In this course, a key message is kept to how many words or fewer?
hints: It is a number that fits in one breath.
The limit is a round number between 15 and 25.
It is the number the course used earlier in this lesson.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The working limit is about 20 words.

questions.onCorrect: Twenty words is only a working limit, and shorter is easier to remember.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the example message. The limit is higher.
That is more than a listener can hold. The limit is lower.

questions.prompt: A question contains a loaded premise. Before you answer, what should you do with it?
hints: Repeating the loaded words carries the premise into your voice.
The other option is to put the question in your own neutral words.
questions.onCorrect: Restating the question in neutral terms lets you answer what is fair in it without adopting its accusation.

misconceptions.feedback: Repeating the loaded wording carries the premise into your own voice. The alternative is to put the question in neutral terms.
That skips the question, and a listener hears evasion. The loaded wording should be put in neutral terms and answered first.

choices.label: Repeat it in the questioner's words
Restate it in neutral terms
Go straight to your key message

questions.prompt: Which opening is best for a sceptical technical audience?
hints: A sceptical technical audience wants to check your claim.
Which opening gives them something to check?

acceptedIdeas: A specific measurement and how it was taken
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A specific measurement and how it was taken

choices.label: A moving story about one customer, with no figures
A list of your qualifications and years of experience
A joke about the topic to put the room at ease
A specific measurement and how it was taken

questions.onCorrect: A measurement and its method give this audience something to test, which is what they came to do.

misconceptions.feedback: A story with no data gives a sceptical technical audience nothing to check.
A joke may warm the room, but it does not meet the need of listeners who want to test the claim.
Credentials ask the audience to trust you. This audience would sooner see the evidence.

questions.prompt: A sceptical engineer says, "Show me the measurement." Which of Aristotle's three appeals does the engineer need most?
hints: The engineer wants reasons and evidence.
Ethos is about character and pathos about feeling.
questions.onCorrect: Logos is the appeal to reason and evidence, and for a listener who asks for a measurement it carries most of the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos rests on the speaker's character. The engineer is asking for evidence, which is another appeal.
Pathos works on feeling. The engineer is asking for evidence, which is another appeal.

choices.label: Ethos
Pathos
Logos

questions.prompt: Of 400 complaints, 300 are about late delivery. A story about one late delivery stands for what percentage of all complaints?
hints: Divide the number about late delivery by the total.
300 ÷ 400 is a decimal.
Write the decimal as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Three in four is a strong basis for the story, so it can stand for the pattern. A story about one of the other 100 complaints would stand for only a quarter.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of late-delivery complaints. Divide it by the total of 400 to get a percentage.
That is the share that are not about late delivery. The question asks for the share that are.

questions.prompt: The last part of a talk, which names exactly what the audience should do next, and by when, is called what?
hints: It is the ask at the end of the arc.
It is a call to do something.
questions.onCorrect: A call to action is specific: it names the step and the time, so the audience knows exactly what to do.

misconceptions.feedback: A conclusion or summary restates the talk. The part that names the next step and the time has another name.

questions.prompt: A 2-minute pitch has 30 seconds on what is, 30 on what could be, 30 for a story used as evidence and 15 for the call to action. How many seconds are left for the opening?
hints: Convert the 2 minutes to seconds.
Add the four slots: 30, 30, 30 and 15.
Take the total of the slots away from 120.
questions.onCorrect: Fifteen seconds is enough to say who you are speaking to and what you want, and no more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the four slots. The opening gets what is left of the 120 seconds.
That is one of the slots. The opening gets what is left once all four are taken from the 120.

questions.prompt: A 3-minute pitch has 40 seconds on what is, 40 on what could be, 50 for evidence and 20 for the call to action. How many seconds are left for the opening?
hints: Convert the 3 minutes to seconds.
Add the four slots.
Take that total away from 180.
questions.onCorrect: Thirty seconds is a comfortable opening for a 3-minute pitch, with room for one sentence of context and one of purpose.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the four slots. The opening gets what is left of the 180 seconds.
That is one of the slots. Take all four away from the 180.

questions.prompt: You are pitching a 3-month trial of an AI drafting tool to a manager. Which call to action is best?
hints: A good call to action names a step and a time.
Which option tells the manager exactly what to do?

acceptedIdeas: Approve the 3-month trial at Monday's meeting.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Approve the 3-month trial at Monday's meeting.

choices.label: Approve the 3-month trial at Monday's meeting.
Support the idea.
Think about trying it.
Let's all do better.

questions.onCorrect: It names the step, approving the trial, and the time, Monday's meeting, so the manager knows exactly what to do next.

misconceptions.feedback: That names no step and no time, so the manager can agree without doing anything.
That names no step and no time. It is a wish and not an ask.
That asks for sympathy and not for a step, so the manager would not know what to do.

questions.prompt: Which of Aristotle's three means of persuasion rests on the character of the speaker?
hints: It is the one about the speaker.
The other two are pathos and logos.
questions.onCorrect: Aristotle says that a speaker persuades by character when they come across as credible, which he traces to good sense, good moral character and goodwill.

misconceptions.feedback: Pathos works on the feelings of the audience. The means that rests on the speaker's character has another name.
Logos is the appeal to reason and evidence. The means that rests on the speaker's character has another name.

questions.prompt: Of 250 complaints, 200 are about late delivery. A story about a late delivery stands for what percentage of all complaints?
hints: Divide the late-delivery complaints by all complaints.
200 ÷ 250 is a decimal.
Write the decimal as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Four in five is a representative basis for the story.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of late-delivery complaints. Divide it by the 250 to get a percentage.
That is the share that are not about late delivery. The question asks for the share that are.

questions.prompt: A speaker tells one unusual case and offers it as proof of a general claim. Is the story working as evidence or as decoration?
hints: Does the story stand for the usual cases?
An unusual case does not represent the others.
questions.onCorrect: A story is evidence only if it is representative and tied to the claim. An unusual case moves the audience without supporting the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: A story is evidence only if it stands for the usual cases. An unusual case does not.

choices.label: Evidence
Decoration

questions.prompt: Programme B has a one-in-three chance of saving all 600 people and a two-in-three chance of saving none. If the same gamble were run many times, about how many people would it save on average?
hints: Picture the gamble run three times.
About one run in three saves everyone and the other two save nobody.

choices.label: About 600
About 300
About 200
None

questions.onCorrect: Over many runs, all 600 are saved about one time in three, which averages out at about 200 a run.

misconceptions.feedback: 600 is what B saves when the one-in-three chance comes off, and two times in three it saves nobody, so the average is well below 600.
300 would be the average if saving everyone and saving nobody were equally likely, but saving nobody is twice as likely.
B saves nobody two times in three, but the third time it saves all 600, so over many runs the average is above zero.

questions.prompt: Programme D has a one-in-three chance that nobody dies and a two-in-three chance that all 600 die. What is the expected number of deaths?
hints: Multiply each outcome by its probability.
Two thirds of 600, plus one third of 0.
questions.onCorrect: Four hundred deaths is exactly what Programme C offers for certain, so C and D are the same in expectation.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the expected number saved. The question asks for deaths, which weights 600 by two thirds.
That is the worst outcome. Multiply it by its probability of two thirds.

questions.prompt: When the same outcomes described as gains or as losses lead people to choose differently, what is the effect called?
hints: The wording is the frame around the same facts.
The effect is named for what the wording does.
questions.onCorrect: The numbers are the same in both wordings, so the change in choices comes from the frame alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Scarcity is an influence principle about limited supply. The effect of wording the same outcomes as gains or losses has another name.

questions.prompt: A seller says "Only 3 left" when 40 are in stock. Which of Cialdini's principles is being abused?
hints: The seller invents a shortage.
Which principle is about limited supply?
questions.onCorrect: Scarcity is honest when the shortage is real and manipulation when it is invented, because the listener cannot check it.

misconceptions.feedback: Authority concerns trusted experts. The seller is inventing a limit on supply.
Liking concerns affinity with the speaker. The seller is inventing a limit on supply.
Reciprocity concerns returning a favour. The seller is inventing a limit on supply.

questions.prompt: Which of these fails the transparency test?
hints: Ask whether you would be comfortable with the listener seeing how and why you used the technique.
Which option depends on the listener not knowing something?

acceptedIdeas: Saying "Only 3 seats left" when 40 are free.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Saying "Only 3 seats left" when 40 are free.

choices.label: Telling a true story about a real customer who was helped.
Quoting a relevant expert on a drug's side effects.
Telling a customer, truthfully, that most of their neighbours pay on time.
Saying "Only 3 seats left" when 40 are free.

questions.onCorrect: The invented shortage works only if the listener does not know it is invented, so it would not survive being seen.

misconceptions.feedback: A true statement about neighbours can be shown openly, so it passes the test.
A true story about a real case can be shown openly, so it passes the test.
Quoting a relevant expert can be shown openly, so it passes the test.

questions.prompt: A surgery is described as having a 90 percent survival rate. Out of 200 patients, how many do not survive?
hints: The non-survival rate is 100% minus 90%.
questions.onCorrect: Ninety percent survives and ten percent does not, and 20 patients is the same fact seen from the other frame.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number who survive. The question asks for those who do not.
That is the percentage who do not survive. Take 10 percent of 200.

questions.prompt: A programme has a one-in-five chance of saving 90 people and a four-in-five chance of saving none. What is the expected number saved?
hints: Multiply each outcome by its probability.
One fifth of 90, plus four fifths of 0.

You want shade because trees cool the street, and I agree it is hot. I hadn't known how much they cool it. My worry is the watering.
