questions.prompt: A team's impact is smaller than the other side's, but it arrives next year and is almost certain. Which weighing sentence is best?
hints: A good weighing sentence concedes what is true and compares on named axes.
Which option names probability and timeframe?

acceptedIdeas: Theirs is larger, but ours is likelier and comes next year.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Theirs is larger, but ours is likelier and comes next year.

questions.onCorrect: It concedes the other side's size, and then names the axes, probability and timeframe, on which the team's impact is stronger.

choices.label: Ours is smaller, but a small impact is still better than none.
Theirs is larger, but ours is likelier and comes next year.
Theirs will not happen, so it should count for nothing here.
Ours matters more, because it feels more real to the people involved.

misconceptions.feedback: That concedes the size but names no axis, so the judge has nothing to weigh.
That treats the other side's impact as nothing, which is rarely believable and easy to rebut.
Emotion is not an axis of comparison. The judge needs size, probability, timeframe or reversibility.

flashcards.front: What word names the statement a speaker wants you to accept?
flashcards.back: The claim is the statement the whole speech is built to make you accept.

flashcards.front: The word because appears in both explanations and arguments. How can you tell which one a speaker is giving?
flashcards.back: Ask whether the listener already accepts the fact being given a cause: if so it is an explanation, and if not the speaker is arguing.

flashcards.front: A listener says "You're wrong" to a speaker. Why does that give the speaker little to answer, and what should the listener name instead?
flashcards.back: It names no part of the argument, so the speaker can only repeat the claim, whereas a challenge to the grounds or the warrant points at something specific.

flashcards.front: What is Toulmin's name for words like "presumably" and "probably" that set how strongly a claim is made?
flashcards.back: A qualifier says how strong the claim is, and a bold claim with weak support is the easiest to push on.

flashcards.front: What do we call a reply that answers the speaker as a person instead of answering the argument?
flashcards.back: An ad hominem answers the person, which leaves the argument itself untouched.

flashcards.front: You have spotted a fallacy in someone's argument. Why does that not show that their conclusion is false?
flashcards.back: It shows that one reason for the conclusion fails, and the conclusion may still be true on other grounds.

flashcards.front: A risk rises from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. What is the relative change, in percent?
flashcards.back: The rise is 1 in 1,000, which is 1 ÷ 2 = 50 percent of the starting risk.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 1 in 1,000, which is 1 ÷ 2 = 50 percent of the starting risk.

flashcards.front: Which question catches most misleading statistics, and what does it ask for?
flashcards.back: Compared with what asks for the starting figure, the group or the base rate that makes the number meaningful.

flashcards.front: Write the strongest five-sentence version of a view you reject. Would someone who holds it say you had put it fairly?
flashcards.back: A fair restatement shows you understood and makes your reply harder to dismiss.

flashcards.front: What do we call the strongest fair version of the other side's case?
flashcards.back: A steelman is the strongest version of a view, stated so that its holder would accept it.

flashcards.front: What do the four letters of PREP stand for, in order?
flashcards.back: Point, Reason, Example, Point: the answer first, why, a case, and the answer again.

flashcards.front: About how many words does a speaker say in one minute, as a planning figure?
flashcards.back: About 150 words a minute is a common planning figure, and speakers vary around it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About 150 words a minute is a common planning figure, and speakers vary around it.

flashcards.front: Record a 60-second talk, count your words and fillers, and replace your most common filler with a pause. Rate the second recording against the first.
flashcards.back: Counting before and after shows whether a change worked, which feelings alone can't.

flashcards.front: A talk of 4 minutes contains 12 fillers. How many fillers a minute is that?
flashcards.back: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 fillers a minute.

flashcards.front: Record yourself answering six tough questions about your own view, 30 seconds each. Rate whether each answer dealt with the question before it bridged.
flashcards.back: A bridge only works once the question has had a real answer, and the recording is how you check.

flashcards.front: In ABC, what do you call the short phrase that moves from your answer to your message?
flashcards.back: The bridge is a short phrase, used once, that follows a real answer.

flashcards.front: Record a 2-minute pitch for a view of yours that ends in one specific call to action. Would the audience know exactly what to do next?
flashcards.back: A call to action names a step and a time, and a recording lets you hear whether yours does.

flashcards.front: What three things does an audience analysis ask about the listeners, before it asks what they will do?
flashcards.back: It asks what they know, what they want and what they fear.

flashcards.front: A plan is described as saving 200 of 600 people. How many does it let die?
flashcards.back: The two descriptions are the same fact: 600 − 200 = 400.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two descriptions are the same fact: 600 − 200 = 400.

flashcards.front: Why does a technique being effective not make it ethical?
flashcards.back: The test is honesty and respect for the listener's judgement, and manipulation often works because it hides what it is doing.

flashcards.front: In a 7-minute British Parliamentary speech, in which minutes may points of information be offered?
flashcards.back: Points of information are allowed only between the protected first and last minutes, so minutes 2 to 6.

flashcards.front: How many teams take part in a British Parliamentary debate, and how many speakers are in each?
flashcards.back: Four teams of two: Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government and Closing Opposition.

flashcards.front: Record a 4-minute case for a motion and score it from 1 to 5 on role, matter, manner and time. Where did you score lowest?
flashcards.back: A score on each criterion shows what to change in the next recording.

flashcards.front: What four axes can you weigh two impacts on?
flashcards.back: Magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility.

essays.title: A councillor's speech sorted and signposted
essays.prompt:
Sort the speech below into its claim, its reasons and the evidence for each, and pick out the one sentence that explains a fact instead of arguing for the claim. Then rewrite the speech so that a listener could follow it at first hearing. Your version will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

A councillor gave this speech at the public meeting, in this order.

Last summer we closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays. Footfall went from 4,000 to 5,000. Thirty-six of the sixty shops took more money and nine took less. There was one injury on those Saturdays, where there had been four on the twelve before. The street was quiet in August because half the town was away. So we should close Market Street to cars every Saturday. Shops do better, and people are safer.
essays.expectedScope: A short sorted list, one sentence on the explanation, and a speech of 70 to 110 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: States the claim in one sentence, and it is the statement the rest of the speech supports.
Gives two reasons and puts the right evidence under each.
Picks out the sentence that explains an accepted fact and says why it does no work for the claim.
The rewritten speech puts the claim first, marks each reason with a spoken signpost and returns to the claim at the end.
The rewrite keeps the councillor's figures unchanged.

essays.title: Three questions for the weak link
essays.prompt:
Find the weak link in the argument below. State the warrant it leaves unsaid, write three closed questions you would put to the speaker, and then rewrite the claim with a qualifier that the evidence can carry. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write the questions exactly as you would ask them.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

The argument, from a councillor: "Footfall on Market Street rose from 4,000 to 5,000 on the trial Saturdays, so closing the street every Saturday will bring a thousand more customers all year."

The trial ran from the middle of June to the end of August. The summer fair was held on the street on two of the twelve Saturdays, and the footfall counter does not tell a customer from someone walking through.
essays.expectedScope: A warrant, three questions and a rewritten claim: 80 to 140 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: States the warrant as a general rule that the argument needs and never says.
One question tests whether the facts are true and complete, one tests whether they support the claim, and one raises a condition under which the rule fails.
Each question can be answered with yes, no or a number.
The rewritten claim carries a qualifier, and the qualifier matches a limit of the trial.

essays.title: Replies to four remarks from the floor
essays.prompt:
Write a reply to each of the four remarks below, as you would give it from the chair of the meeting. Each reply has two parts, the first saying in plain words what the remark did and the second taking the meeting back to the question. Your replies will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday. The chair of the traders' association, who owns a furniture shop, has spoken against the closure. A councillor has spoken for it.

(1) "Of course she is against it. She sells sofas."

(2) "The councillor wants to ban cars from Alderby."

(3) "Either we close the street or we watch the town centre die."

(4) "My neighbour's shop took less on those Saturdays, so the trial was bad for the shops."
essays.expectedScope: Four replies of two sentences each: 100 to 170 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: Each reply says in plain words what the remark did, and the description fits that remark.
No reply relies on a label alone, such as a Latin name, to make its point.
Each reply ends by returning the meeting to a question about the closure that can be checked.
At least one reply grants that the speaker's conclusion might still be right for other reasons.
Each reply is short enough to say in one breath.

essays.title: The trial's numbers said fairly
essays.prompt:
Write the part of a speech that reports the trial's results to the public meeting, fairly enough that neither side could call it slanted. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

These are the trial's figures. Saturday footfall on the street rose from 4,000 people to 5,000. Of the street's 60 shops, 36 took more money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 9 took less, and those 9 mostly sell furniture, appliances and garden supplies. There was 1 injury on the street during the twelve trial Saturdays and there had been 4 on the twelve Saturdays before. Traffic on Mill Lane, the next street, rose from 300 vehicles an hour to 420. Eight parking bays for blue badge holders were out of use, and the nearest others are 250 metres away. Barriers and two stewards cost £900 each Saturday.
essays.expectedScope: A passage of 110 to 170 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Gives the rise in footfall as a number of people and as a percentage of the starting figure, and both are right.
Gives the shops that gained and the shops that lost as shares of the 60.
Reports the injuries without claiming more than counts of four and one can show, and says why.
Gives the change on Mill Lane, so that the cost to the next street is in the account.
Names one comparison that the trial did not make and a careful listener would ask for.

essays.title: A steelman and a rebuttal of the traders' case
essays.prompt:
You are speaking for the closure, straight after the speech below. Restate the traders' case so fairly that its speaker would accept your version, say where you agree, and then rebut it with one move. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

The chair of the traders' association said this: "Nine shops took less money, and they are the ones that sell what you cannot carry home on foot. Eight blue badge bays went out of use, and the nearest are 250 metres away. Mill Lane took 420 vehicles an hour where it had taken 300. The barriers and stewards cost £900 every Saturday. Leave the street open."

You also know that 36 of the street's 60 shops took more money on the trial Saturdays and that footfall rose from 4,000 to 5,000.
essays.expectedScope: A reply of 120 to 190 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: Restates the traders' case with its strongest point included, in words its speaker would accept.
Names a point of agreement before any criticism.
Makes one rebuttal, and a reader can tell whether it denies the evidence, denies the link, gives an exception, or concedes and outweighs.
Concedes something specific, with its figure.
Gives reasons for your own claim and does not ask the traders to disprove it.

essays.title: A one-minute answer, written out
essays.prompt:
The chair of the meeting turns to you and asks: "Should Market Street be closed to cars every Saturday?" Write the answer you would give in one minute, in favour or against, using the PREP pattern. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

These are the trial's figures. Saturday footfall on the street rose from 4,000 people to 5,000. Of the street's 60 shops, 36 took more money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 9 took less, and those 9 mostly sell furniture, appliances and garden supplies. There was 1 injury on the street during the twelve trial Saturdays and there had been 4 on the twelve Saturdays before. Traffic on Mill Lane, the next street, rose from 300 vehicles an hour to 420. Eight parking bays for blue badge holders were out of use, and the nearest others are 250 metres away. Barriers and two stewards cost £900 each Saturday.
essays.expectedScope: An answer of 135 to 165 words, which is about a minute at 150 words a minute. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: Opens with the answer to the question and closes by returning to it.
Gives a reason and then an example that uses a figure from the trial.
Is between 135 and 165 words long.
Marks its parts with spoken signposts and holds no more than three points.
Is written for the ear: no sentence is too long to say in one breath, and no figure appears that a listener could not repeat.

essays.title: A rehearsal note on pace and nerves
essays.prompt:
Write yourself a note after the rehearsal described below. Work out your pace and your filler rate, say how many words the script has to lose, choose one target for the next run, and say how you will handle the nerves. The note is written work and will be read here, not heard.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday. You have a slot of two minutes at the public meeting.

You rehearsed once with a timer and a friend. Your script has 390 words and you got through all of it in exactly 2 minutes. Your friend counted 14 fillers such as "um" and "you know", and said that the three figures in the middle went past too fast to catch. You plan at 150 words a minute. Your heart was racing before you began.
essays.expectedScope: A note of 90 to 150 words. Allow about 8 minutes.
successCriteria: Gives the pace and the filler rate of the rehearsal, both worked correctly from the figures.
Says how many words the script must lose to fit two minutes at the planning pace.
Chooses one target for the next rehearsal and says how it will be measured.
Says where a pause would help and what job the pause does there.
Handles the nerves in the way the lesson's research supports, and does not claim more for it than the research does.

essays.title: Answers to three hard questions
essays.prompt:
You have spoken for closing Market Street every Saturday, and the questions begin. Write your key message, and then your answer to each of the three questions below. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday. Of the street's 60 shops, 36 took more money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 9 took less. The trial ran only in summer, and nobody has measured Mill Lane, the next street, in winter.

(1) "Did any shop take less money during the trial?"

(2) "Why are you so determined to kill off the furniture shops?"

(3) "What will this do to the traffic on Mill Lane in December?"
essays.expectedScope: A key message and three answers of two or three sentences each: 100 to 170 words. Allow about 12 minutes.
successCriteria: The key message is 20 words or fewer and says what you want the listener to keep.
The first answer gives its yes or no, with the figure, before anything else.
The second answer does not repeat the question's loaded words in your own voice.
The third answer says what you do not know and what you will do about it.
Each answer reaches the key message by a bridge that follows from what was asked.

essays.title: One opening for two rooms
essays.prompt:
You will make the case for closing Market Street to two audiences in one week: the traders' association on Tuesday and the town's disability access forum on Thursday. Write a line of audience analysis for each, and then the opening of each talk. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

These are the trial's figures. Saturday footfall on the street rose from 4,000 people to 5,000. Of the street's 60 shops, 36 took more money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 9 took less, and those 9 mostly sell furniture, appliances and garden supplies. There was 1 injury on the street during the twelve trial Saturdays and there had been 4 on the twelve Saturdays before. Traffic on Mill Lane, the next street, rose from 300 vehicles an hour to 420. Eight parking bays for blue badge holders were out of use, and the nearest others are 250 metres away. Barriers and two stewards cost £900 each Saturday.

A trader you spoke to, who runs the bakery, sold out by noon on eight of the twelve Saturdays. A forum member you spoke to uses a wheelchair and gave up on one trial Saturday when the nearest bay was full.
essays.expectedScope: Two lines of analysis and two openings of 60 to 90 words each. Allow about 15 minutes.
successCriteria: For each room, says what the audience knows, wants and fears, and what you want them to do afterwards.
The two openings lead with different things, and each difference follows from the analysis.
Earns trust by what it shows of your grasp of the audience's concern, without a list of your credentials.
Any story stands for a pattern in the figures, and the figure is given with it.
Each opening ends by asking the audience for one specific thing.

essays.title: One fact in two frames
essays.prompt:
Write the fact below twice, once framed by what was gained and once by what was lost, and say which side of the debate would choose each. Then deal with the colleague's line that follows, and write the sentence you would be willing to say yourself. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

The fact: of the street's 60 shops, 9 took less money on the trial Saturdays, 15 took about the same and 36 took more.

A colleague on your side, who wants the closure, plans to say: "Every other market town in the county has already done this." Two of the county's seven market towns have.
essays.expectedScope: Two framed sentences, a note on the colleague's line and a sentence of your own: 90 to 150 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: The two framed sentences state the same fact, and the numbers or percentages in both are right.
Says which side would choose each frame and why.
Names the principle of influence in the colleague's line and says what would make its use honest.
Applies the transparency test to a wording of your own and says what the test shows.

essays.title: Preparation notes for the fifth speech
essays.prompt:
The Alderby question has become a debating motion, and you are the Member for the Government in a British Parliamentary round. Write your preparation notes: where your team stands, the extension you will bring, a point of information to offer, and your plan for the points offered to you. The notes are written work and will be read here, not heard.

The motion is "This House would close town-centre shopping streets to cars every Saturday". Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

The Opening Government has argued that shops take more money and that fewer people are hurt. The Leader of the Opposition has just said that the nine Alderby shops which took less money prove that closures harm trade. In Alderby, 36 of 60 shops took more and 9 took less.
essays.expectedScope: Four short notes: 90 to 150 words. Allow about 10 minutes.
successCriteria: Says which teams you are trying to outrank, including the one on your own side, and where your speech comes in the order.
States an extension in a sentence, and it is a line of argument that the Opening Government's two points do not cover.
The point of information is one question or one point, short enough to say in about 15 seconds.
Says when in a speech a point may be offered and how many you plan to accept in your own.

essays.title: An extension built and weighed
essays.prompt:
Build the argument you would bring as a closing Government speaker, and weigh it against the Opposition's strongest impact. Write three lines of motion analysis, then the argument as a claim, a mechanism and an impact, then the weighing. Your answer will be read here and not heard, so write out the words you would say.

The motion is "This House would close town-centre shopping streets to cars every Saturday". Alderby and its figures are invented, and this course's tasks all argue over them. Last summer the council closed Market Street to cars on twelve Saturdays, from 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon, and it now has to decide whether to close it every Saturday.

Use the extension you chose in the last lesson's task. If you skipped it, use this one: a closed street serves the people in a town who do not drive, a group the Opening Government never mentioned. In Alderby, an invented survey on the trial Saturdays found that 300 of the 1,000 extra visitors were under 17 or over 75.

The Opposition's strongest impact is on blue badge holders. Eight bays were out of use on each trial Saturday, about 40 badge holders would have used them over the day, and the nearest other bays are 250 metres away.
essays.expectedScope: Three lines of analysis, an argument and its weighing: 150 to 230 words. Allow about 15 minutes.
successCriteria: The motion analysis says what the motion asks, who the actors are and what each side has to show.
The argument states a claim and then a mechanism that explains how the claim would come about.
The impact says who is affected and how much, with a figure.
The weighing compares the two impacts on at least two named axes.
The weighing treats the Opposition's impact as real and says why yours still weighs more, or what change to the policy would meet it.
